== Problem 18==
A rhombic dodecahedron is a solid with <imath>12</imath> congruent rhombus faces. At every vertex, <imath>3</imath> or <imath>4</imath> edges meet, depending on the vertex. How many vertices have exactly <imath>3</imath> edges meet?

<imath>\textbf{(A) }5\qquad\textbf{(B) }6\qquad\textbf{(C) }7\qquad\textbf{(D) }8\qquad\textbf{(E) }9</imath>

== Solution 1 ==
Note Euler's formula where <imath>\text{Vertices}+\text{Faces}-\text{Edges}=2</imath>. There are <imath>12</imath> faces. There are <imath>24</imath> edges, because there are 12 faces each with four edges and each edge is shared by two faces. Now we know that there are <imath>2-12+24=14</imath> vertices. Now note that the sum of the degrees of all the points is <imath>48</imath>(the number of edges times 2). Let <imath>x=</imath> the number of vertices with <imath>3</imath> edges. Now we know <imath>\frac{3x+4(14-x)}{2}=24</imath>. Solving this equation gives <imath>x = \boxed{\textbf{(D) }8}</imath>. ~aiden22gao ~zgahzlkw (LaTeX) ~ESAOPS (Simplified)

== Solution 2 ==
Let <imath>x</imath> be the number of vertices with 3 edges, and <imath>y</imath> be the number of vertices with 4 edges. Since there are <imath>\frac{4*12}{2}=24</imath> edges on the polyhedron, we can see that <imath>\frac{3x+4y}{2}=24</imath>. Then, <imath>3x+4y=48</imath>. Notice that by testing the answer choices, (D) is the only one that yields an integer solution for <imath>y</imath>. Thus, the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }8}</imath>.

~Mathkiddie

== Solution 3 ==
With <imath>12</imath> rhombi, there are <imath>4\cdot12=48</imath> total boundaries. Each edge is used as a boundary twice, once for each face on either side. Thus we have <imath>\dfrac{48}2=24</imath> total edges.

Let <imath>A</imath> be the number of vertices with <imath>3</imath> edges (this is what the problem asks for) and <imath>B</imath> be the number of vertices with <imath>4</imath> edges. We have <imath>3A + 4B = 48</imath>.

Euler's formula states that, for all convex polyhedra, <imath>V-E+F=2</imath>. In our case, <imath>V-24+12=2\implies V=14.</imath> We know that <imath>A+B</imath> is the total number of vertices as we are given that all vertices are connected to either <imath>3</imath> or <imath>4</imath> edges. Therefore, <imath>A+B=14.</imath>

We now have a system of two equations. Solving the system yields <imath>A=\boxed{\textbf{(D) }8}</imath>.

Even without Euler's formula, we can do a bit of answer guessing. From <imath>3A+4B=48</imath>, we take mod <imath>4</imath> on both sides.

<cmath>3A+4B\equiv48\pmod{4}</cmath><cmath>3A\equiv0\pmod{4}</cmath>

We know that <imath>3A</imath> must be divisible by <imath>4</imath>. We know that the factor of <imath>3</imath> will not affect the divisibility by <imath>4</imath> of <imath>3A</imath>, so we remove the <imath>3</imath>. We know that <imath>A</imath> is divisible by <imath>4</imath>. Checking answer choices, the only one divisible by <imath>4</imath> is indeed <imath>A=\boxed{\textbf{(D) }8}</imath>.

~Technodoggo ~zgahzlkw (small edits) ~ESAOPS (LaTeX)

== Solution 4 ==
Note that Euler's formula is <imath>V+F-E=2</imath>. We know <imath>F=12</imath> from the question. We also know <imath>E = \frac{12 \cdot 4}{2} = 24</imath> because every face has <imath>4</imath> edges and every edge is shared by <imath>2</imath> faces. We can solve for the vertices based on this information.

Using the formula we can find:<cmath>V + 12 - 24 = 2</cmath><cmath>V = 14</cmath>Let <imath>t</imath> be the number of vertices with <imath>3</imath> edges and <imath>f</imath> be the number of vertices with <imath>4</imath> edges. We know <imath>t+f = 14</imath> from the question and <imath>3t + 4f = 48</imath>. The second equation is because the total number of points is <imath>48</imath> because there are 12 rhombuses of <imath>4</imath> vertices. Now, we just have to solve a system of equations.<cmath>3t + 4f = 48</cmath><cmath>3t + 3f = 42</cmath><cmath>f = 6</cmath><cmath>t = 8</cmath>Our answer is simply just <imath>t</imath>, which is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }8}</imath> ~musicalpenguin

== Solution 5 ==
Each of the twelve rhombi has two pairs of angles across from each other that must be congruent. If both pairs of angles occur at <imath>4</imath>-point intersections, we have a grid of squares. If both occur at <imath>3</imath>-point intersections, we would have a cube with six square faces. Therefore, two of the points must occur at a <imath>3</imath>-point intersection and two at a <imath>4</imath>-point intersection.

Since each <imath>3</imath>-point intersection has <imath>3</imath> adjacent rhombuses, we know the number of <imath>3</imath>-point intersections must equal the number of <imath>3</imath>-point intersections per rhombus times the number of rhombuses over <imath>3</imath>. Since there are <imath>12</imath> rhombuses and two <imath>3</imath>-point intersections per rhombus, this works out to be:

<imath>\frac{2\cdot12}{3}</imath>

Hence: <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }8}</imath> ~hollph27 ~Minor edits by FutureSphinx

== Solution 6 (Based on previous knowledge) ==
Note that a rhombic dodecahedron is formed when a cube is turned inside out (as seen here), thus there are 6 4-vertices (corresponding to each face of the cube) and 8 3-vertices (corresponding to each corner of the cube). Thus the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }8}</imath>

== Solution 7 (Dual) ==
Note that a rhombic dodecahedron is the dual of a cuboctahedron. A cuboctahedron has <imath>8</imath> triangular faces, which correspond to <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }8}</imath> vertices on a rhombic dodecahedron that have <imath>3</imath> edges.

== Solution 8 (Uses Solution 2)==
Continue through solution 2 until you get <imath>3x+4y=48</imath>. Then we have that <imath>3x = 48-4y = 4(12-y) = \text{multiple of 4}</imath> so <imath>x</imath> is a multiple of <imath>4.</imath> The only multiple of 4 answer choice is <imath>8 = \boxed{(D)}</imath>

~KindToucan
